name: data-access-object
intent: Abstract and encapsulate all access to one particular data store behind a store-specific interface whose methods speak in domain terms, so business code never sees the store's API, dialect, connection handling or vendor error codes and the quirks of that store stay in one place.
problem: Business objects talk to the store directly, embedding SQL, driver calls, connection handling and vendor error codes in ordinary application code: the application is coupled to one vendor's dialect and API, the same persistence details are duplicated across components, the store cannot be substituted (for a test, a second vendor or a replica) without editing business logic, and no single place can enforce access rules.
context: Applications that must reach a persistent store whose API is proprietary or vendor-specific - a relational database, a directory, a flat file, a legacy or remote service - especially when that store may later be swapped, reached through a second path (batch job, replica, cache) or faked in tests. It presupposes a language with interfaces, protocols or duck typing, and it is a decision about the access boundary only: the pattern says nothing about how domain objects are mapped, which is the separate concern of Data Mapper, Active Record or Table/Row Data Gateway.
benefits: Business objects become independent of the store implementation: the same client code works when the DAO is backed by the relational database today and by an in-memory, message-based or second-vendor implementation later.

All store-specific knowledge - SQL dialect, driver calls, connection handling, row mapping, vendor error codes - is centralised in one place per aggregate, so schema or vendor changes touch the DAO layer alone.
The interface is a natural test seam: an in-memory or stub implementation replaces the store, so business logic is exercised without a database and slow tests are avoided.
Failure semantics can be normalised: the DAO translates vendor exceptions into the application's own error types, keeping error handling and retry policy consistent across stores.
Access rules get a single choke point: parameter binding, statement limits, audit logging and timing can be enforced where all access to that store passes through.
New callers cannot invent their own SQL: the domain-level interface is the only vocabulary available to business code, which keeps access patterns reviewable.
tradeoffs: It adds a layer: an interface, at least one implementation per store, transfer objects, and usually the same find/add/update/delete plumbing re-written for every aggregate, so small applications pay more structure than they save.
The abstraction leaks: an in-process interface cannot hide that each call may be a slow round trip, so callers still cause N+1 patterns and chatty access through innocent-looking method calls.

Abstraction inversion is a real failure mode: designing the DAO's methods around what the store does well (row sets, cursors, vendor extensions) forces callers to know store details in order to pick a method.

A DAO sees only its own store, so transaction boundaries and object identity across several DAOs need a Unit of Work or Identity Map above it; without that, partial writes and duplicated in-memory copies appear.
Exception translation is easy to skip, letting vendor exceptions (SQLException, SqliteError, driver-specific codes) escape into business code and silently re-couple it to the store.
Using a DAO factory adds a parallel class hierarchy of factories and products to design and keep in sync, which Oracle's own consequence list names as an extra cost.
When a full ORM or data mapper is already in place, a per-aggregate DAO often degenerates into a pass-through that adds indirection without hiding anything.
In async contexts, the DAO must be explicitly async-aware; exposing synchronous blocking calls on an async interface defeats the purpose of async and leaks concurrency complexity to callers.

participants.responsibility: The data client: a component that needs the data and calls the DAO interface, knowing nothing about the store's API, dialect or connection handling.
The store-agnostic contract for one aggregate: domain-level operations (find, add, update, delete, query) plus the error types callers may see.
The store-specific class or module that owns the connection or pool, executes statements, maps rows and translates vendor errors - the only place the store's API appears.
The store itself (relational database, directory, file, remote service) together with the driver and pool that reach it.
The carrier accepted and returned across the boundary: a plain data structure or domain value, so no handle, cursor or result set escapes.
Optional: creates the concrete DAO (or a family of DAOs) for a chosen store when the store must be selected at run time.

use_cases: An application that must run against more than one relational vendor, or against an embedded database in tests, keeps one DAO interface per aggregate and one implementation per vendor.
A legacy or third-party data source - mainframe, LDAP directory, SOAP/HTTP service, flat file - whose nonstandard API must not spread into business code.
A component that reaches the same store through a second path (bulk loader, nightly job, read replica) and needs the same domain-level operations as the online path.
Persistence code that stores domain objects as rows while business code must stay free of SQL and result sets, including hand-written mapping on top of a driver.
Test suites that need a fast in-memory or stub implementation behind the same interface so business logic can be exercised without a database.
Access layers that must enforce a policy (audit logging, tenant filtering, statement limits) at one place for every caller.
Microservices that own their own data store and expose it only through a typed interface, keeping service boundaries strict and enabling independent schema evolution.
CQRS read-model projections where the read side needs a denormalised view; a dedicated DAO isolates the projection logic from the command-side persistence.
Applications using async/await frameworks (FastAPI, asyncio) where data-access calls must be non-blocking and the DAO interface is naturally async.

Android apps using Room persistence: interfaces annotated @Dao declare insert/update/delete and @Query methods, and Room generates the implementation at compile time with SQL validated against the schema, so raw SQLite access never reaches view models.

Spring applications on JDBC, Hibernate or JPA use Spring's DAO support: DAO classes annotated @Repository get technology-specific exceptions (SQLException, HibernateException) translated into Spring's unified DataAccessException hierarchy, so one error-handling style works across persistence technologies.

Java services generated with jOOQ enable DAO generation to obtain a typed org.jooq.DAO per table (findById, exists, deleteById, per-column fetch methods) used as a base class underneath hand-written queries.
avoid_when: The application talks to exactly one store through a framework that already provides the data access layer (Spring Data repository, EF Core DbContext, ActiveRecord, a mature ORM): a DAO on top is indirection without isolation.
A full data mapper or ORM is the chosen mapping strategy - use its gateway or repository and keep domain logic out of SQL instead of hand-writing DAOs beside it.
The access pattern really varies per query or per report: a query object, query builder or plainly named SQL functions stay simpler than a per-aggregate interface.
The data lives in the language's own collections or an embedded key-value store with the same API - the standard library is already the interface.
A throwaway script, migration or CRUD admin screen: one parameterised helper is enough, and the extra layer is pure ceremony.
anti_patterns: "God DAO": one class with a method per query for the whole schema, so the interface changes with every screen and can never be implemented a second time.
Leaky DAO: methods that return result sets, cursors, data readers or vendor error codes, leaving clients coupled to the store the pattern was meant to hide.
DAO that also enforces business rules (validation, workflow, authorisation decisions), merging the two responsibilities the boundary exists to separate.
A single DAO instance shared globally, holding mutable connections or state across threads without pooling or synchronisation.
Copying the same generic CRUD interface for every aggregate while business code still needs dozens of query methods - the duplication the pattern is rightly criticised for.
Adding a DAO layer on top of an ORM that already exposes an equivalent repository, producing a pass-through that hides nothing.
Returning ORM-managed entities or proxy objects from DAO methods, exposing persistence lifecycle and causing runtime errors outside the owning transaction.
Exposing synchronous blocking I/O in an async context, defeating the async event loop and turning every DAO call into a potential concurrency bottleneck.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: store access is one concern, business decisions another; the DAO owns only the former.
Program to an interface, not an implementation: clients depend on the DAO contract, never on the concrete store class.
Information hiding: the store's API, dialect and error codes do not cross the DAO boundary.
Single responsibility per role: interface, implementation, factory and transfer object each have one job.
Dependency inversion: the consuming layer defines the contract it needs, while concrete DAOs (and a factory) supply it.
Testability as a design goal: the seam exists so the store can be replaced by a test double without touching business logic.

Domain vocabulary principle: DAO method names should reflect what the caller wants (findPendingOrders, findByEmail) not how the store retrieves it (selectWhereStatusEquals). This keeps the interface stable across store migrations.
best_practices: Name the interface in domain terms (findCustomerByEmail, not selectFromCustomers) so implementations stay interchangeable.
Return plain values or transfer objects - never drivers' result sets, cursors or connections.
Translate vendor exceptions into the application's own error types inside the DAO; keep SQLException, SqlError and driver codes out of business code.
Inject the connection or pool (or a session factory) rather than opening connections per call, and let the pool own connection lifetime.
Give one DAO one aggregate or table, and select the implementation with dependency injection or a factory rather than conditionals in callers.
Keep transaction boundaries out of individual DAO methods when several DAOs participate; let a Unit of Work or the service layer own the boundary.
Always bind parameters inside the DAO so injection safety is enforced at the single choke point, and cap statement results where the store allows it.

Prefer batch and bulk operations (addMany, updateMany, deleteMany) over looping single-item calls, to reduce round-trips and keep the DAO the single choke point for query optimisation (eager loading, join strategies).
In async codebases, make DAO methods explicitly async and use async-aware drivers; never perform blocking synchronous I/O inside an async interface as it starves the event loop.
Use eager loading strategies (selectinload, joinedload, batch fetching) or dedicated aggregate-fetch methods (findOrderWithItems) to prevent N+1 query generation when traversing related entities.
Expose paginated result methods (findAll(page, size) or similar) rather than returning unbounded result sets that stress the store and the network.
Add loader options or query hints as parameters to the DAO method rather than spreading fetch strategy decisions across service-layer callers.
sources: Alur, Crupi & Malks, Core J2EE Patterns: Best Practices and Design Strategies, 2nd ed. (2003) - Data Access Object pattern chapter, the definitive J2EE specification of the pattern with factory integration.

Martin Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (PoEAA), 2002 - DAO appears across the catalog; Fowler's site at martinfowler.com/eaaCatalog documents Table Data Gateway, Row Data Gateway, Data Mapper, Repository and Active Record as related/alternative patterns.
Martin Fowler, 'Catalog of Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture', https://martinfowler.com/eaaCatalog/ - online reference for Repository, Data Mapper, Unit of Work, and related patterns.

Oracle Java Technology Documentation, 'Design Patterns: Data Access Object', https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/dataaccessobject.html - Oracle's canonical Java tutorial on DAO pattern structure and factory integration.
XUnitPatterns.com, 'Data Access Object', http://xunitpatterns.com/Data%20Access%20Object.html - testing perspective on DAO as a test seam, with notes onFake DB implementations.
Wikipedia, 'Data access object', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_access_object - general reference with historical note on Sun Java Center.
Baeldung, 'The DAO Pattern in Java', https://www.baeldung.com/java-dao-pattern - modern Java practitioner's overview of DAO usage, benefits and common mistakes.

Baeldung, 'DAO vs Repository Patterns', https://www.baeldung.com/java-dao-vs-repository - clarifies the distinction and layering between DAO (lower-level, data-centric) and Repository (higher-level, domain-oriented collection).
Kamenik Solutions, 'Data Access Object', https://kameniksolutions.com/garden/data-access-object/ - practical notes on N+1 pitfalls, abstraction leakage, and real-world DAO design signals.

Tomoda Hinata, 'SQLAlchemy 2.0 Practical Guide: Designing a Type-Safe ORM Data-Access Layer', https://tomodahinata.com/en/blog/sqlalchemy-2-typed-orm-production-guide - Python/SQLAlchemy perspective on repository/DAO pattern, async considerations, loader strategies and transaction boundaries.

SQLAlchemy ORM Documentation - AsyncIO section, https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/21/orm/extensions/asyncio.html - best practices for async DAO implementations in Python with AsyncSession lifecycle management.

Stack Overflow, 'What is the difference between DAO and Repository patterns?', https://stackoverflow.com/questions/8550124/what-is-the-difference-between-dao-and-repository-patterns - community-accepted answer distinguishing DAO (data/persistence-centric, table-oriented) from Repository (domain-oriented, collection-like, aggregate-focused), with Unit of Work notes.

Medium / Ahmet Emre Demirşen, 'DTO vs DAO: The Most Confused Concepts in Spring Boot', https://medium.com/but-it-works-on-my-machine/dto-vs-dao-the-most-confused-concepts-in-spring-boot-5103b912703b - DAO abstraction leakage pitfalls in Spring Boot, DTO vs entity distinction, N+1 mitigation.

Core J2EE Patterns (Sun Java Center), 'Data Access Object', http://corej2eepatterns.com/DataAccessObject.htm - the canonical DAO definition: uniform API over diverse data sources (RDBMS, LDAP, OODB, XML, flat files) with the noted cost of an added abstraction layer and a DAO class hierarchy to maintain.

Android Developers, 'Access data using Room DAOs', https://developer.android.com/training/data-storage/room/accessing-data - official guide to @Dao interfaces and abstract classes: Room generates implementations at compile time and validates @Query SQL, the pattern's most widely deployed modern use.

Spring Framework Reference, 'DAO Support', https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/reference/data-access/dao.html - official documentation of @Repository-enabled exception translation across JDBC, Hibernate and JPA into one DataAccessException hierarchy: a production implementation of the DAO error-normalisation responsibility.

jOOQ Manual, 'DAOs', https://www.jooq.org/doc/latest/manual/sql-execution/daos/ - official documentation of code-generated typed DAO<R, P, T> classes per table (findById, exists, count, per-column fetches) with the stated limit of single-column primary keys.

Yegor Bugayenko, 'DAO is Yet Another OOP Shame', https://www.yegor256.com/2017/12/05/data-access-object.html - criticism: DAOs plus data-carrier entities turn domain objects into anemic data containers and make handling procedural.

jOOQ blog, 'Like repositories, jOOQ's DAOs are only useful for very simple stuff', https://blog.jooq.org/to-dao-or-not-to-dao/ - criticism from a vendor whose own DAO feature is optional: the generic CRUD API invites quick access over thoughtful query design; keep DAOs as a thin base layer.

Pavel Samolysov, 'The Controversial DAO Pattern', http://psamolysov.blogspot.com/2015/11/the-controversial-dao-pattern.html - criticism: swapping the store behind a DAO (ORM to JDBC, relational to NoSQL) rarely avoids touching business logic because transaction and synchronization guarantees differ.

related_patterns_notes.table-data-gateway: Table Data Gateway is a narrower variant: one gateway object exposes all operations for a single database table or view, where DAO typically wraps an aggregate or domain concept. DAO often delegates to a Table Data Gateway internally while adding domain-language naming, error translation and transaction awareness.
related_patterns_notes.row-data-gateway: Row Data Gateway wraps a single row as an object; a DAO implementation may use a Row Data Gateway for each row returned, but DAO adds the interface boundary and aggregation of multiple row operations into a cohesive API.
related_patterns_notes.dao-factory: DAO Factory creates families of concrete DAO implementations for different stores, enabling runtime selection of the data source. It is an optional participant that complements DAO without being a replacement.
related_patterns_notes.data-mapper: Data Mapper handles bidirectional object-to-database translation independently of access patterns, while DAO provides the access interface. In systems that use Data Mapper for O/R mapping, DAO typically sits above it as the calling convention; the mapper is an implementation detail of the DAO.
related_patterns_notes.repository: Repository is a higher-level, domain-oriented collection abstraction that typically sits above DAO in a layered architecture. Where DAO is close to the data source and may expose multiple query methods for a table or aggregate, Repository presents a collection-like interface (add, remove, find) for domain objects and often coordinates with a Unit of Work. A Repository commonly delegates to one or more DAOs internally; the two patterns compose rather than compete.
related_patterns_notes.data-transfer-object: Data Transfer Object (DTO) is the data carrier that crosses the DAO boundary. The DAO receives DTOs as input and returns them as output, so no store-specific object (result set, cursor, connection) leaks to callers. DTO and DAO are thus complementary: DTO is the data shape, DAO is the access contract.
related_patterns_notes.unit-of-work: Unit of Work tracks changes made to objects loaded by a DAO and persists them atomically at transaction boundaries, solving the problem of multi-DAO partial writes. Without a Unit of Work, each DAO method must independently commit, risking inconsistency. DAO provides the per-aggregate access; Unit of Work provides the transactional coordinator across DAOs.
related_patterns_notes.identity-map: Identity Map ensures each in-memory object is loaded only once, preventing duplicate instances from appearing after separate DAO queries. When multiple services call the same DAO for the same entity key, Identity Map keeps them seeing the same instance; it is a companion to DAO for maintaining object identity within a session or request.
